Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 1:

Surah al-Haqqah (سُورَةُ الحاقَّةِ)

It is Meccan, and its verses number fifty-two, without disagreement regarding either of these two matters. What indicates the first is what Imam Ahmad narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I went out intending to confront the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before I embraced Islam, but I found that he had preceded me to the mosque, so I stood behind him. He began reciting Surah al-Haqqah, and I began to marvel at the composition of the Qur'an. By Allah, this is a poet! He then recited: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Haqqah: 41]. I said: 'A soothsayer!' He said: ﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember. [It is] a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Haqqah: 42–43], to the end of the surah. Then Islam entered my heart in every place."

When the mention of the Day of Resurrection had occurred in general terms in Nun, Allah, glorified is He, explained in this noble surah the account of that Day and its great matter, and included within it the mention of the conditions of nations that denied the messengers, peace be upon them, and what befell them, so that those contemporary deniers of the Prophet (ﷺ), may blessings and peace be upon him, might be restrained. The Mighty One, the Lord of Majesty, said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Al-Haqqah﴾: that is, the Hour, or the Reality that is certain and must occur (يَحِقُّ ويَجِبُ وُقُوعُها), or the one in which the true matters of reckoning, reward and punishment are established and confirmed, or the one in which matters are known in their reality (تُعْرَفُ عَلى الحَقِيقَةِ), from "ḥaqqahu, yuḥiqquhu," when one knows its reality. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and others. Attributing the verb to it under the last two interpretations is metaphorical (مَجازٌ), while it is literal (حَقِيقَةٌ) with respect to the matters in it or to the people of knowledge in it. In al-Kashf, it is stated that the attribution is metaphorical only under the last interpretation.

As for the second interpretation, it also admits metaphorical attribution, because establishment and obligation belong to what is in it. It may also be intended that it means "the one possessing the Reality," by way of naming a thing with the name of what accompanies it. This is more probable, because the Hour and what is in it are equal in the obligation of their establishment, so the indication for metaphorical attribution weakens, and the figurative usage here is depiction and emphasis. End of quotation.

Al-Jalabi discussed this with what is open to discussion, so return to it and reflect. Al-Azhari said: ﴿Al-Haqqah﴾ is the Resurrection, from "ḥaqaqtuhu, fa-ḥaqqaqtuhu," meaning I contended with him and overcame him. Thus it is "al-ḥaqqah" because it overcomes every contender against the religion of Allah, the Exalted, through falsehood, that is, every opponent, so it prevails over him. The apparent sense of their words is that, in all of this, it is an adjective whose noun has been omitted, to indicate the full clarity of its being characterized by this attribute and its functioning as a proper name. It has also been said that, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, it is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection, a fixed noun (اسْمٌ جامِدٌ) that is not considered as an adjective with an omitted noun. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (مَصْدَرٌ), like al-ʿAqibah and al-ʿAfiyah. Whatever the case, it is a subject (مُبْتَدَأٌ) whose predicate is the sentence

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 2:

﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [It is said that] "ma" is the subject (mubtada') and "al-Haqqah" is the predicate (khabar), or the reverse; the meaning favours [the reverse]. The first [arrangement] is the well-known one, and the link (al-rabit) is the repetition of the subject with its own wording. The original form would be "ma hiya," meaning: "What is it, in its state and attribute?" For "ma" may be used to ask about the attribute and the state. The apparent noun has therefore been placed in the position of the pronoun, to magnify its matter and to make its affair awe-inspiring.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 3:

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ That is, "What thing has made you know what it is?" This is an emphasis on its awfulness and dreadfulness, by explaining that it lies beyond the sphere of the knowledge of created beings. The meaning is that its greatness and the extent of its terror and severity are such that the understanding of no one nearly reaches it, nor does their imagination. However you imagine its state, it is beyond that, and greater, and greater still, so informing about it is not possible. From this it is known that the interrogative was used as a metaphor for its necessary implication, namely that it is not known, and the perception of no dwelling reaches it, and the imaginations and thoughts do not attain it. The word "ma" (what) is in the nominative position as the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the verb "idrak" (made to know). There is no room here for the reverse. The phrase "wa ma al-Haqqah" (and what is the Inevitable Reality) is a clause in the accusative position, by dropping the preposition, not that "adra" (to make know) takes a second object with "bi" (with), as in His saying ﴿nor would He have made you know of it﴾ [Yunus: 16]. Since the interrogative clause came as a suspending clause for the verb, it occupies the position of the second object. The suspension of this verb, it is said, is because it contains the meaning of knowing. The clause, i.e., "what made you know" and so on, is conjoined to the preceding clause of the smaller clauses.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 4:

﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ The Striking Calamity (al-Qari'ah) is the Day of Resurrection, which strikes people with terror and dread, and the heaven with splitting and cleaving, and the earth and the mountains with crushing and scattering, and the stars with effacement and dispersal. He placed it in the position of a pronoun referring to ﴿al-Haqqah﴾ to indicate the meaning of striking, which is the striking of one thing against another, in order to intensify its terror. The sentence is a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new sentence that begins an independent statement) brought to explain some of the conditions of al-Haqqah. For him (ﷺ), the effect of its clarifications: ﴿What could make you know what it is?﴾ No one knew it (ﷺ), and the clarifying element is that it is of such a nature that it is right for those who deny it to be destroyed. As if it were said: ﴿And what could make you know what al-Haqqah is?﴾ Thamud and 'Ad denied it, so they were destroyed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 5:

﴿Then as for Thamud, they were destroyed﴾, meaning: Allah destroyed them. Zayd ibn Ali read «fa-halakū» (they perished) with the active form of the verb, ﴿by the al-ṭāghiyah﴾, meaning the event that exceeds the limit, which is the Cry (al-ṣayḥah), in accordance with His saying, exalted is He, in [Hud: 67] ﴿And the Cry seized those who did wrong﴾. By it was also interpreted the thunderbolt (al-ṣāʿiqah) in Ḥā Mīm al-Sajdah, or the earthquake (al-rajfah), in accordance with His saying, glorified is He, in [al-A'raf: 78, 91] / (﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾). The earthquake is the tremor caused by the Cry. There is therefore no contradiction among the verses, because the attribution in some of them is to the immediate cause and in others to the remote cause. The first (view) is related from Qatadah, who said: that is, by the Cry that went beyond the limit of every cry. Ibn Abbas, Abu Ubayda and Ibn Zayd said something to the effect that al-ṭāghiyah is a verbal noun (maṣdar), so it is as if it were said: by their transgression. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thamud denied in their transgression﴾ [al-Shams: 11]. But the one relied upon is the first, because of the saying of Allah, exalted is He,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 6:

﴿And as for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a screaming, furious wind.﴾

The clarification of this is that the verse contains both combination and separation. If it were said, "These were destroyed by rebellion (al-ṭughyān), as a attracting cause (sabab jālib), and those by the wind, as an instrumental cause (sabab ālī)," there would be no correspondence (ṭibāq), since it would be permissible for these [the second group] also to have perished because of rebellion. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhsharī's (d. 538 AH) statement weakening the second [reading] for lack of correspondence between it and ﴿bi-rīḥin﴾ (by a wind). Not because one of them is a substance (ʿayn) and the other an event (ḥadath); and the support mentioned for this does not hide its condition.

Likewise, the first [reading] is preferred over the view of Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd as well, that is, because of the rebellious deed they committed, which was hamstringing the she-camel. It has been said that "al-ṭāghiyah" is the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and the ta' in it is for emphasis, as in "rajulun rāwiyah" (a man who narrates much). They were all destroyed because of his deed, since they approved of his action. It has also been said: because of the rebellious group (al-fi'ah al-ṭāghiyah). The basis for preferring the first is known from what has been mentioned. The discussion of ṣarṣar has already passed, so reflect on it. It is an attribute of wind. Similarly is His statement, exalted is He, ﴿ʿātiyah⦆ (furious), meaning intensely violent in its blast, or it rebelled against ʿĀd, so they were unable to repel it or to escape it by any stratagem, such as concealing themselves in a building, seeking refuge in a mountain, or hiding in a pit, for it would uproot them from their places and destroy them. Rebellion (ʿutūw) in both senses is a metaphor; its origin is transgressing the limit, and it may be in relation to another or may not be, and from this the difference between the two aspects is known.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, may Allah honour his face, that he said: No drop ever descended except by measure, through the hands of an angel, except on the day of Noah, for He permitted the water without the treasurers, so the water rebelled against the treasurers and went out. That is the meaning of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, when the water rebelled﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11]. And no wind descended except by measure, through the hands of an angel, except on the day of ʿĀd, for He permitted it without the treasurers, so it went out. That is the meaning of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿with a screaming, furious wind﴾, which rebelled against the treasurers.

This is found in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and Muslim and others, which agrees with it, so it is a transmitted (ma'thūr) explanation. This has been reported in al-Kashshāf, then he said: "Perhaps it is an expression for its intensity and excess." It was explained in al-Kashf as a metaphorical allegory (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah), then he said: When a proverb reaches the point where the intended meaning is understood from it without looking at the origin of the story, it is permissible to say that it is a metonymy (kināyah) for it, as in what we are discussing. He also permitted that there be an eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh) from ʿutūw, which is departing from obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He subjected it against them﴾, etc., is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought in to explain the manner of their destruction by the wind. It is also permissible that it be another attribute (sifah), and that it was brought in to negate what might be suspected: that the wind was a result of the conjunctions of some stars with others and their descent into certain mansions (manazil). For if the conjunctions that necessitate certain events did exist, that would be by His decree and causation, Exalted and Glorified is He, not from their own essences independently. The cause that the naturalists (al-tabi'iyyun) mention for the wind is the condensation of air in the direction toward which it moves, and the piling of some of it upon other parts, by a drop in its degree of heat, so that its expansion decreases and it condenses and leaves most of the place that was occupied empty; or by a sudden gathering that occurs in the vapours dispersed in the air, so that their places become empty.

In either case, the neighbouring air rushes toward that place with force to fill it. This continues until that expanse is filled and the air within it becomes balanced, and then it becomes still. Its movement varies in speed and slowness. According to what has been said, a moderate wind covers about one farsakh in an hour, a medium one about four farsakhs, a strong one about eight farsakhs, and what is stronger than that about sixteen farsakhs. What is stronger still, and is called the mu'tafikah, covers about twenty-nine farsakhs, and it may cover thirty-six farsakhs in an hour. This is the greatest that has been said regarding the speed of the wind.

They have made an instrument which they claim is a measure by which the strength and weakness of the blowing of the wind can be known, and this is not far from the human kind. What they have mentioned as the cause is to be answered in the manner of what you have just heard. The meaning of ﴿He subjected it against them﴾ is that He, Mighty and Majestic, empowered it over them by His power. ﴿Seven nights and eight days, in succession (husuman)﴾ means: successive, as Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu 'Ubaydah said. It is the plural of ḥāsim, like shuhud, the plural of shahid, from ḥasamtu al-dabbah when you repeat cauterizing the animal for a disease, time after time, until it is eradicated (yanḥasim). So it is a metonymic usage (majaz mursal) of the restricted (muqayyad) sense, namely the ḥasm which is the successive cauterizing, for absolute succession. In al-Kashf it is said that it is a metaphor taken from ḥasm in the sense of cauterizing: the days are likened to the one who cauterizes, and the wind, because of its association with them, its blowing in them, and the continuation of its description with their description, as in their saying "a cold day" and "a hot day," and so on, by the action of the days; each gust of them is a cauterization, and their succession is by the succession of the cauteries, until the eradication (inḥisam), that is the uprooting of the disease, which is the aim, occurs.

The meaning after summarizing: successive blowings of the winds, until they reached them and uprooted them; or ill-omened, unlucky ones, as al-Khalil said. It was said that the meaning is "cutting off good by their ill-fortune and ominousness," so the object of ﴿husuman﴾ is omitted; or "cutting off," meaning they cut off their last remnant and destroyed them to the last one, as Ibn Zayd said.

Al-Raghib said: ḥasm is the removal of the trace of a thing; it is said: "he cut it, and so eradicated it," that is, removed its root. By it the sword was named ḥusam. Ḥasm of a disease is the removal of its trace by cauterizing. It was also said that ill-omen which removes the trace of what it has struck is called ḥusum. As for ﴿husuman﴾ in the verse, it was said: "eradicating their trace"; it was said: "eradicating their news"; it was said: "cutting off their lives." All of these fall within its generality, so do not be heedless.

It is also permissible that ḥusuman be a verbal noun (maṣdar), not a plural of ḥāsim, and its accusative status is either by its implied verb as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal), meaning "by eradicating them with eradication," i.e., you uproot them with uprooting; or as an accusative of purpose (ʿillah), meaning "He subjected it against them for the sake of eradication"; or it is an attribute, meaning "possessing eradication."

The verbal-noun reading is supported by the reading of al-Suddi, "ḥasūman" with a fatḥah on the ḥa', as a circumstantial accusative from the wind, meaning: He subjected it uprooting them, since its being a singular noun is then determined in that way. These were the days of the "old woman" (ʿajuz), from dawn on Wednesday, eight days remaining of Shawwal, until sunset of the following Wednesday. They were called "the days of the old woman" because an old woman of 'Ad hid herself in a cave, and the wind tore her out on the eighth day and destroyed her; or because they are the "buttocks" (ʿajuz) of winter, so ʿajuz means ʿajuz (the rear). Their names are: al-Ṣann, al-Ṣanbar, al-Wabr, al-Amir, al-Mu'tamar, al-Mu'allil, Mutfi' al-Jamr, and Mutfi' al-Ẓaʿn. Whoever said they are seven, not eight, did not mention this eighth, as is the preferred view. ﴿Then you see the people﴾: that is, if you were present at that time, the address is to him; ﴿in it﴾: that is, in the days and nights; it was also said: in the directions of the winds; it was also said: in their homes; the first is more apparent. ﴿Overthrown (ṣarʿa)﴾: that is, destroyed, the plural of ṣarīʿ. ﴿As if they were trunks of palm trees﴾: that is, the roots of palm trees. Abu Nahik read "aʿjaz" on the pattern of af'al, like ḍabʿ and aḍbaʿ; al-Akhfash related that it was read "nakhil" with a yā'. ﴿Hollow﴾: their insides were emptied out by decay and corruption. Ibn Shajarah said: [the wind] would enter through their mouths and bring out what was inside their bodies, the contents of their bellies, through their posteriors, so they became like hollow palm trunks.

Yahya ibn Salam said: their bodies were emptied of their spirits, so they were in that state. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: they were under punishment for seven days, then on the eighth they died, and the wind threw them into the sea; this is His saying, Exalted is He.

﴿So do you see any remnant of them?﴾ That is, any remainder. This may be understood as: the word "bāqiyah" is a noun like "baqiyyah" (remnant), not an adjective, and the "tā'" serves to shift it into the nominal category; or as: a remaining self/person, with an implied noun modified, and the "tā'" being the feminine marker. Ibn al-Anbari said: it means "bāq" (remaining), and the "hā'" is for intensification (mubalaghah). He also permitted that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "ṭāghiyah" and "kādhibah," meaning "baqā'" (lasting), and the "tā'" is for unity (waḥdah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 9:

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him﴾: those before him from the sinful nations, such as the people of Noah (peace be upon him). Within this is a generalization after specification, for among them were ʿAd and Thamud. Abu Rajaʾ, Talha, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan (in one of the reports from him), ʿAsim (in the narration of Aban), al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians, al-Kisaʾi and Hamza, in the narration of ...), and Aban read ﴿wa-man qablahu﴾ with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning "and those in his direction and side," and the intended meaning is "those with him from among his followers and the people of his obedience." This is supported by the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud: "wa-man maʿahu" (and those with him).

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: that is, the towns of the people of Lut (peace be upon him). The intended meaning is their inhabitants, either metaphorically by using the name of the place for those who dwell in it, or by an implied omitted noun, and by metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). The indicator (qarinah) is the conjunction with those who are described as having come. Al-Hasan read here "wal-mu'tafikatu" in the singular.

﴿with the sin﴾: that is, with the error, taking it as a verbal noun on the pattern of fa'ilah; or with the deed, or with the deeds possessing great error. The attribution is metaphorical, while it is literally true of its doers. The mention of greatness is because an act is not made erroneous unless its doer is extremely erring. It is also permissible for the form to be one of attribution (li-l-nisbah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 10:

﴿فَعَصَوْا رَسُولَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ That is: "so each nation disobeyed its messenger" when he forbade them from the abominations they were engaged in. Thus, the singular "messenger" (rasul) is to be taken in its apparent sense. It is also permissible that it be a plural, or a noun that applies equally to the singular and the plural, since it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) and is intended for multiplicity, as the context requires. Thus it stands in contrast to the plural, which implies the division of individuals. Or the singular may be used for them collectively, since they are unified in meaning regarding that with which they were sent. The apparent meaning is that this is an explanation of their coming with the sinful deed. ﴿فَأخَذَهُمْ﴾ That is, Allah, mighty and majestic, ﴿أخْذَةً رابِيَةً﴾ That is, an seizing increased in severity, just as their abominations increased in ugliness, from "rabā al-shay'" (the thing increased) when it grew.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 11:**

﴿When the water rose beyond its usual limit,﴾ it exceeded its customary bound, so that it rose above the highest mountain by fifteen cubits. Or it overflowed its reservoirs, as you have heard shortly before. This was because of the persistence of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, in various kinds of disbelief and sin, and their great insistence in denying him, peace be upon him, regarding what was revealed to him of the rulings, among which are the conditions of the Resurrection. ﴿We carried you﴾ i.e., in the loins of your fathers; or We carried your fathers while you were in their loins. This is on the basis of an omitted noun (taqdir mudaf). It has also been said that the address is figurative, meaning your fathers who were carried, by the relation of containment (ʿalaqah al-hulul), but this is far-fetched. ﴿In the sailing ship﴾ i.e., in the ship of Noah, peace be upon him. The meaning of carrying them in it is raising them above the water until the days of the Flood ended, not merely lifting them into the ship, as the word (fi) indicates. For (fi) is not connected to the verb "carried," but is related to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its object. The sense is: "We raised you above the water and preserved you while you were in the sailing ship, by Our command and Our protection."

**Page 43**

In this there is an indication that the basis of their salvation was purely the protection of the Mighty and Majestic, and that the ship was only an apparent means. The word *jariyah* (sailing) is often used for a ship, and it is said that there were ninety *jariyah* within the belly of a *jariyah*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 12:

﴿So that We may make it﴾ i.e., the act, which is an expression for the deliverance of the believers and the drowning of the disbelievers, ﴿a reminder for you﴾ (tadhkirah), a lesson and a sign of the perfection of the Maker's power, His wisdom, the strength of His dominion, and the vastness of His mercy, ﴿and that a retaining ear may retain it﴾ (ta'iyaha), i.e., preserve it. Al-wa'y (retention) means that you preserve a thing within yourself, while al-i'da' (depositing) means that you preserve it outside yourself, in a vessel (wi'a').

﴿a retaining ear﴾, i.e., it is of its nature to preserve what must be preserved, by remembering it, spreading it, reflecting upon it, and not losing it by abandoning acting upon it.

And from Qatadah: "The retaining one is the one that understood from Allah the Exalted and benefited from what it heard of the Book of Allah the Exalted." And in a report: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may Allah honour his face: 'I have asked Allah the Exalted that it be your ear, O 'Ali.'" 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "I never heard anything and then forgot it, and it was not for me to forget."

In attributing retention to the ear, and likewise making it preserving and remembering and the like, there is a metaphor (tajawwuz). The one who performs that is in fact its owner, and in reality only the hearing is attributed to it. The indefinite form (al-tankir) is used to indicate its paucity, and that one whose condition is this, along with [the one] being killed for a cause, [serves] for the deliverance of the great multitude and the continuation of their progeny.

It is said that the pronoun in "We may make it" refers to the ship (al-jariyah), and that making it a reminder is because, as Qatadah said, the first of this community encountered it, i.e., they saw its planks on al-Judi, as Ibn Jurayj said.

Indeed, it has been said that some people found some of its remnants long after Islam, but Allah the Exalted knows best its soundness, and it is not hidden that what is relied upon is what we have already presented.

Ibn Musarrif and Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Harun and Kharijah from him, and it is said with a difference from him, recited "wa-ta'iyaha" (وتَعْيَها) with the 'ayn sukun, by analogy with kathif and kabid, as has been said. Hamzah recited with the kasrah made faint (ikhfa' al-kasrah). It is narrated from 'Asim that he recited with shaddah on the ya'. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it is said this is an error, and it should be interpreted as meaning the clarification of the ya' (shadd bayan al-ya') to guard against one who would make it sakin, not the idgham of one letter into another; and it should not be considered doubling in pause, then the connected reading treated as the pause, though some have gone to this.

It is narrated from Hamzah and Musa ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Absi "wa-ta'iyaha" (وتَعِيَها) with the ya' sukun, which permits that it is a new sentence (isti'naf), which is the apparent reading, and permits that it be like the reading of "min awsat ma tut'imuna ahlikum" with the ya' sukun. Nafi' recited "udhun" (أُذْنٌ) with the dhal sukun for lightness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 13:

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast﴾. This begins the explanation of the Inevitable Reality (al-Haqqah) itself and the manner of its occurrence, following the explanation of its great importance through the destruction of those who denied it. By "the single blast" is meant the first blast, at which the destruction of the world occurs, as Ibn 'Abbas said. Ibn al-Musayyib and Muqatil said it is the final blast. The first view is preferable, because it suits what follows, although the conjunction "wa" (and) does not indicate sequence; yet departing from the apparent meaning without a reason is unnecessary. As for "nafkhah" (blast), Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) said in the marginal notes of his Kashshaf: "The 'marrah' (single instance) and its indication of blowing is incidental and not intended, and the occurrence of the great matter by it and after it is magnified only in terms of the blowing occurring once, not in terms of it being a blowing. Therefore He, glorified be He, drew attention to this with His words ﴿single﴾."

Ibn al-Hajib related that "nafkhah" was not established to indicate unity in itself; rather it was established to indicate blowing, and the indication of unity is incidental and not intended. It has been objected that this, even if granted, does no harm, because the discussion concerns what the context requires, not the original lexical establishment. It has been affirmed that what the speech is directed toward is treated as the principal element, to the extent that other things are set aside. Thus "marrah" (single instance) is the principal element in view of the context, rather than the blowing itself, even though a look at the apparent wording would suggest the reverse. So understand.

In any case, the attribution of the verb to "nafkhah" is not like the attribution of the verb to an emphatic verbal noun, as in "daraba darban" (he struck a blow), even if one does not consider what follows in His words ﴿single﴾. It also justifies the masculine form of the verb because of the separation, and because the subject is not truly feminine and is a verbal noun. The well-known view is that ﴿single﴾ is an emphasizing adjective, though some called it emphasis and others called it clarification. Al-Tibi mentioned that the followers (tawabi') such as the apposition (badal), the explanatory apposition ('atf al-bayan), and the adjective are, according to the rhetoricians, a kind of clarification of the thing followed in one respect. **Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 14:**

﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted﴾. They are raised from their places by the mere power of God, without any created intermediary, or through the agency of something such as a wind or an angel, it is said. Or through the agency of an earthquake (*zalzalah*), meaning that the earthquake has some role in the raising, not that the earth is itself the one raising them and carrying them, so that someone could say that there is no carrying in it and that it is only agitation. It is also said that God, exalted is He, may create from the heavenly bodies (*al-ajram al-'ulwiyyah*) something that has the power to pull the mountains and lift them from their places. Or there may be, in the bodies that exist today, something that has the power for this, except that there is an obstacle between them preventing the pulling and the raising, and that this obstacle will later disappear, so the raising takes place. Likewise, it is permissible to consider something similar in relation to the earth, and for the forces of the two attracting bodies to be different. So when the raising of each reaches an end that God, exalted is He, intends, there occurs in that attracting body a change, such that the attraction no longer remains with it, through the removal of its alignment (*musamtihi*) or the like, and between the mountains and the earth there arises what necessitates collision.

It is also permissible that God may bring about in the earth forces that necessitate its hurling the mountains, and may bring about for the earth itself what necessitates its being raised from its place. That among these forces some are mutually repellent and some mutually attractive is something that is hardly to be denied. It is also said that their raising may be by the collision of some bodies, such as comets (*dhawat al-adhnab*), according to what has been said about them, against the earth, so that the mountains separate and are raised because of the severity of the collision.

As for the raising of the earth from its place, it is not hidden that all of this, despite its being what it is, is not needed, and that it suffices us to say that the raising is by the power of God, which nothing can resist.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Ibn Muqsam, al-A'mash and Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Yahya, read «وحُمِّلَتِ» with a doubled *mim*. It is taken as indicating multiplicity (*al-takthir*). It is also permitted that it be an intensification of the transitive form (*tadh'if lil-naql*), so that «الأرْضُ والجِبالُ» is the first object, raised to the position of the subject, and the second object is omitted, meaning "power," or "wind," or "angels," or it may be that the second object is raised to the position of the subject and the first is omitted, and it is one of the things mentioned.

﴿So they will be pounded into one pounding﴾. The two bodies are struck, one against the other, after being raised, with one blow, until they are crushed and return as ﴿a heap of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. It is said that their parts will scatter, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 6]. Scholars have distinguished between *al-dakk* and *al-daqq* by saying that in the first there is scattering of the parts, and in the second there is their differentiation.

One of the eminent scholars (*al-ajillah*) said: The original meaning of *al-dakk* is striking what has risen so that it becomes low, and it necessarily entails leveling in most cases, so the word became common in this sense until it became a literal meaning. From it comes *ardun dakka'* ("a level and spacious land"), *ba'irun adakk* and *naqatun dakka'* when both have become weak, so that their humps do not rise and they become level, and their humps and backs are equal. So what is meant here is that they will be spread out in one spreading and leveled, and will become an earth in which you see no crookedness or unevenness. Perhaps the crumbling is also a preliminary to the leveling.

Al-Raghib said: *al-dakk* is soft and easy ground. God's statement ﴿they will be pounded﴾ means that they are made like soft ground, and this too returns to leveling, as is not hidden.

It is reported in *Majma' al-Bayan* that when they are pounded, the mountains crumble, the wind scatters them, and the earth remains level. The pronoun is in the dual because of the intention of the two sentences, as we have indicated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 15:

﴿Then on that Day﴾ i.e., then at that time, on the basis that by "the Day" is meant time in general, which here is extensive, and in which occurs whatever occurs. ﴿So it﴾, that is, the sky, ﴿on that day will be frail﴾: weak, from "wahā al-shay'", meaning the thing weakened and began to collapse and fall. Ibn Shajara said, from their saying "wahiya al-siqa'" (the water-skin became torn) when it is ruptured. Among their proverbs is the verse of the rajaz poet:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 17:**

﴿And the angel﴾, meaning the kind known as "malak" (angel). According to al-Zamakhshari and a group of scholars, it is more general than "malā'ika" (angels). Al-Jawhari also mentioned this. Abu Hayyan said: "Malak is a collective noun used to mean the angels, and it does not clearly appear to be more general than the angels." The full investigation of this question, with nothing to add to it, is in the commentary on al-Talkhis by al-‘Allama al-Thani and its marginal notes, so return to them if you wish. ﴿Upon its sides﴾, meaning its edges, the plural of *rajā'* (رجى, sides), with a short vowel. It is a word of the *dhawat al-wāw* type (with an original waw), which is why it appears with its waw in the dual. The poet said:

*"As if you had not seen before me a captive in chains, nor a man whom the two sides (rajawān) throw down."*

The pronoun refers to the heaven, and what is meant by its sides is its extremities that have not split. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak that they said: "﴿And the angel upon its sides﴾, meaning upon the parts of it that have not split." Perhaps this is their seeking refuge at the edges, due to what overcame them from observing the greatness of God, exalted and majestic, or because they gather there for the descent.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he said: "﴿And the angel upon its sides﴾, meaning the angels upon its side, looking at the splitting of the earth and what came to them of terror." The first explanation is more apparent. Perhaps this splitting occurs after the death of the angels at the first blast and their revival, for they are revived before people, as the reports indicate. It is also possible that this happens after the second blast, while the people are at the place of gathering. Some reports indicate that every heaven splits on that day and its angels descend. The day is long, as we have pointed out.

Al-Imam said: It is possible that they stand at the edges for a moment and then die. It is also possible that what is meant by them are those whom God, exalted, excepted in His saying: ﴿except whom God wills﴾ [al-Naml: 87; al-Zumar: 68]. Under both interpretations, the objection that the angels die at the first blasting is resolved, based on His saying: ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. So how can it be said that they stand at the edges of the heaven? In Anwar al-Tanzil it is said: Perhaps His saying ﴿and the heaven will be split﴾ and so on is an image of the ruin of the world through the ruin of the structures and the gathering of its inhabitants toward its edges. If it is taken literally, then perhaps the death of the angels follows that. End of quote. I do not say that the image interpretation is possible.

In al-Bahr, from Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak, the pronoun in ﴿its sides﴾ refers to the earth, even though it is not mentioned before. They said: "They descend to it, guarding its edges, just as it is related that God, exalted, commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth. Then the angels of the second heaven, and they line up around them. Then the angels of each heaven. So whenever any of the jinn or humankind tries to flee, he finds the earth surrounded by them." Perhaps what we related from them is more worthy of reliance.

﴿And above them will bear the throne of your Lord﴾, meaning above the angels who are upon the sides, indicated by "the angel." It was also said: above the entire world. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the angels who bear it, meaning they bear the throne of your Lord above their backs or their heads. ﴿On that day, eight﴾. The referent, though it comes later in wording, is prior in rank. The benefit of "above them" is the indication that it is not carried in their hands, like something suspended, for example. This is supported, and the consideration of backs is supported, by what al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related, and Ibn Majah related "on that day, on that day," from al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib in a hadith: "And above that are eight wild goats (awʿāl), between their hooves and their haunches is the distance from one heaven to another. Then above their backs is the throne, the distance between its lower part and its upper part being like the distance from heaven to heaven."

What is meant by the wild goats in it are angels in the form of wild goats, as Ibn al-Athir and others said. It is the plural of *wi‘l* (وعل), with a kasra on the ‘ayn, meaning a mountain ibex. It has been used as evidence that what is meant is eight individuals. The reports indicating this are many, but there is conflict among them, in that some indicate that some of them are in the form of a human, some in the form of a lion, some in the form of a bull, and some in the form of an eagle. Other reports indicate that each of them has four faces: the face of a bull, the face of an eagle, the face of a lion, and the face of a human. And each of them has four wings: two wings on his face, out of fear that he might look at the throne and swoon, and two wings with which he flies. Abu Hayyan did not affirm the authenticity of any of that, saying: "They mentioned in the descriptions of these eight contradictory forms, which we have set aside entirely."

Abd ibn Humayd related from Ibn Zayd, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Today four carry it, and on the Day of Resurrection eight will carry it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he named none of the bearers of the throne except Israfil, peace be upon him. He said: "Mika'il, peace be upon him, is not one of the bearers of the throne." Accordingly, whoever claims that he and Jibril and Izra'il, peace be upon them, are among its bearers must establish that with a report on which one can rely.

From Shahr ibn Hawshab: four of them say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your pardon after Your power," and four say: "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge."

In a report from Wahb ibn Munabbih: "They have no speech except their saying: 'Sanctify God, the Mighty, whose greatness has filled the heavens.'" Most reports on this subject are not to be relied upon.

Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Dahhak that he said: "It is said: eight rows, whose number no one knows except God, exalted and majestic." This statement was also related by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim through several chains from Ibn ‘Abbas.

Al-Hasan said: "God, exalted, knows best how many they are: are they eight categories or eight individuals?" You know that the apparent meaning, supported by some authentic reports, is that they are eight individuals. Whatever the case, the apparent meaning is that there is a literal carrying, and this is the view of Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified. He said: "God, exalted, has angels who carry the throne, which is the couch, on their shoulders. They are four today, and tomorrow they will be eight, for the purpose of carrying it to the land of gathering." He, may his secret be sanctified, has an extensive discussion about the bearers of the throne in the thirteenth chapter of his *Futuhat*, especially regarding its interpretation as kingship. Let whoever has the capacity of mind to understand his words return to it.

He also allowed that this may be an image of the greatness of God, exalted and majestic, by what is witnessed of the states of sultans on the day they come out to the people for a general judgment. Thus what is meant is His manifestation, exalted and majestic, through the attribute of greatness. And he made the presentation (*al-‘ard*) in His saying, exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 18:

﴿On that Day you will be presented (for judgment)﴾ is metaphorical for the reckoning (ḥisāb). What is meant is: on that Day you will be called to account. However, this has been likened to the ruler's presentation of his army (ʿarḍ al-sulṭān al-ʿaskar) in order to know their conditions, and so it has been expressed by it.

Imam Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be presented on the Day of Resurrection three times. As for the first two presentations, they involve disputing and excuses. As for the third, then at that point the scrolls will fly into hands, so one will take his record in his right hand and another will take his in his left."

The clause for which the tanwin is a substitute (al-jumla al-muʿawwaḍ ʿanha al-tanwīn), according to what their speech indicates, is ﴿The Trumpet is blown﴾, and ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾ has been made a substitute for ﴿So on that Day﴾, and so on. You have already heard that the time is broad enough to encompass all that has been mentioned and other things.

As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿no secret of yours will be hidden﴾, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the nominative subject of ﴿you will be presented﴾. That is: you will be presented while nothing of your secrets is hidden from Him, mighty and majestic is He, even before that. The presentation is only for the disclosure of the state, the establishment of proof, and the emphasis on justice. Or (it means): nothing is hidden on that Day from people, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when hidden things are laid bare﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 9].

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Wathhāb, Ṭalḥa, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Miqsam from ʿĀṣim, and others read "lā yakhfā" with the yāʾ (third person masculine), i.e. لا يَخْفى.

﴿Then as for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾: this is a detailed explanation of the rulings concerning the presentation (al-'ard). By "his record" is meant what the angels wrote concerning what he did in the world. They have mentioned that the deeds of each day and night are written in a page, so the pages of a single servant become many. It was said that they are joined together for him, and so he is given them joined. It was also said that everything in all of them is copied into one page, and this is what al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, held firmly. According to both opinions, the word "record" applies to what the servant is given. It was also said that the servant's deeds are written in a book in his grave, and that this is the record he is given on the Day of Resurrection. This is a weak opinion and is not relied upon.

It will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, that there is an explanation of how the servant is given that. ﴿He will say﴾, boasting and showing off, ﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾. Al-Radi said: "Ha" (hā) is a word meaning "take," and it has eight dialects. The first: with an alif alone, unchanging, for the singular, the dual and the plural, masculine or feminine. The second: this lone alif is joined by the letter of address kaf, as in dhalika and its inflections, such as hāka, hākumā, hākum, hākunna. The third: a hamzah is joined to the alif in place of the kaf, and its inflection is like that of the kaf, such as hā'uhā, hā'um, hā'a, hā'umā, hā'unna. The fourth: a hamzah with a fatha is joined to the alif before the kaf of address, and the kaf is inflected as hā' with a sukun hamzah after the hā' for all. The fifth: this phrase is inflected like "da'" (leave). The sixth: its inflection is like that of "khaff" (lighten). The seventh: its inflection is like that of "khaff" (lighten). 

Among this is what al-Kisa'i related from the saying of one who was told "hā'" with a fatha: "ilām ihā'" and "ahā'" with a fatha on the hamzah of the speaker and with a kasra. The eighth: a hamzah is joined to the alif, and its inflection is like that of "nādi" (call). The last three are verbs that do not inflect; they have no past or present tense, and they are not verbal nouns (asma' al-af'al). Al-Jawhari said: "Hā'i" with a kasra on the hamzah means "hāt" (bring), and with a fatha it means "khudh" (take). If you are told "hā'" with a fatha, you say "mā ahā'" meaning "what do I take?", and "mā uhā'" in the passive, meaning "what was given?" This which he said is based on the seventh, like "mā akhāf" and "mā ukhāf." End of quotation.

Abu al-Qasim said: In it there are dialects, the best of which is what Sibawayh related in his book, where he said: "The Arabs say: hā' ya rajul (to a man) with a fatha on the hamzah, and hā'i ya imra'ah (to a woman) with a kasra, and hā'umā ya rajulān or imra'atān (to two men or two women), and hā'um ya rijāl (to men), and hā'un ya niswah (to women)." The mīm in hā'um is like the mīm in antum, and its damma is like its damma in some instances. Here it is explained as "khudhū" (take, plural), which is transitive by itself to the object, and the object is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned, namely ﴿my record﴾, and it is the object of ﴿read﴾. This was chosen over the reverse, because if the object of ﴿hā'um﴾ were it, it would be said "iqra'ūhu," since the better course is to use a pronoun where possible, as here. It did not appear in the first case lest it refer to something later both in wording and in rank. It is in the accusative case, although the governing word, according to the good dialect, is a verb-noun (ism fi'l), so the pronoun is not attached to it.

It was said that "hā'um" means "ta'ālaw" (come), so it would take "ilā." Al-Qutbi claimed that the hamzah is a substitute for the kaf. It was said that this is weak, unless he meant that it occupies its place in some dialect, as you have heard, in which case it is possible, but not that it is a grammatical substitution, because the kaf is not substituted for a hamzah nor a hamzah for it. It was also said: "hā'um" is a word coined for answering the caller at times of joy and enthusiasm.

In a hadith: "A Bedouin called out to him in a loud voice, and he, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, answered him with 'hā'um' in the force of his voice." He allowed the intention of this meaning here, for it is possible that the one given his record in his right hand is called by his relatives and friends, for example, to read his record, and he answers them, out of his great joy and enthusiasm, with the words ﴿Here!﴾. Some people claimed that it is originally compounded: "hā ummū," meaning "aim (at it)," then ease of pronunciation and usage transferred it to what has been mentioned.

Others claimed that the mīm is the pronoun for a group of males, and the hā' in ﴿kitābiyah﴾, and likewise in ﴿ḥisābiyah and māliyah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28], and ﴿sulṭāniyah﴾ [al-Haqqah: 29], and likewise ﴿mā hiyah﴾ in [al-Qari'ah: 10], are for pausing (lil-sakt, a brief silent pause) and not a pronoun of the third person. Therefore it should be dropped in continuous reading (wasl) and kept in pausing (waqf), so that the vowel of the word pausing on it is preserved. When one continues, one dispenses with it. Among them, some kept it in continuous reading, treating it as pausing, or because he continued with the intention of pausing. The readings differ. The majority read with it, both in continuous reading and in pausing.

Al-Zamakhshari said, following the Imam codex (al-Mushaf al-Imam, the standard written copy of the Qur'an). Ibn al-Munir criticised him, saying: "Reducing the reading to following the codex is strange, given that the true belief is that the readings, in all their details, are transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ." He elaborated at length in censuring it. He was right in what he said. Ibn Muhaysin read with dropping it in both continuous reading and pausing, and the yā' in the words mentioned with sukun. This is not reported for ﴿mā hiyah﴾ in what I have checked. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash read with dropping the hā' in them in continuous reading but not in pausing. Hamzah dropped it in ﴿māliyah﴾ and ﴿sulṭāniyah﴾ and ﴿mā hiyah﴾ in continuous reading, but not in pausing, and with a fatha on the yā' in them. What al-Zahrawi said, that keeping the hā' in continuous reading is a solecism which no one I know of permits, is nothing, for it is widely transmitted (mutawatir), and so it is obligatory to accept it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 20:

﴿Indeed, I thought that I would encounter my reckoning.﴾ That is, I acted accordingly, as most of the scholars have said, on the basis that what is apparent in the state of the believer is certainty regarding the matters of the Hereafter, such as the reckoning. Therefore, what is reported from him should be the same, but theoretical matters, because their details are not free from some hesitation, do not undermine certainty in them, such as the ease or severity of the reckoning, for example. He expressed knowledge with "thought" as a figurative usage (majaz (figurative usage)) to indicate this.

It has also been said that since belief in the matters of the Hereafter in general is not free from anxious thoughts and mental impulses (khataraat), like all theoretical sciences, it was placed in the position of thought and he expressed it with it for this reason. This indicates that such (fluctuation) does not harm faith. It is also permissible that "thought" be in its literal sense, with the meaning of his reckoning being the easy reckoning he received, for certainty about that is not attained by him, and he merely thought it and gave it preference because of his great trust in the mercy of God, Exalted and Majestic. Perhaps that was at the time of death, for the reports indicate that what befits the believer's state at that time is the predominance of hope and good opinion.

As for before death, it is the balance between hope and fear. In light of this it becomes very clear that this sentence falls in the position of giving a reason for what the first sentence implies of good condition. It is as if it were said: "I am in a state that is good, or I am joyful and happy, because I thought well of my Lord, glorified is He, that He would reckon with me an easy reckoning, and He has reckoned with me in that way." So God, Exalted, is according to His servant's opinion of Him. This is better than what has been said: that the meaning may be "I thought that I would encounter my reckoning with severity and strict scrutiny because of the faults that had passed from me, and now God has removed that from me and relieved my distress." It has also been said that "thought" is used for knowledge in its literal sense, and this is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Radi (al-Radi) regarding the verbs of the heart (af'al al-qulub), but there is room for reflection in this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 21:

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: that is, a pleasing (marḍiyya) life. Others said: that is, one possessing contentment (dhāt riḍan), on the basis that it is of the type of attribution by form (nisba bi-l-ṣīgha), like laabin (having milk) and tamir (having dates). Therefore this interpretation is not valid, unless it is said that the taʾ in it is for emphasis (mubālagha). And in this there is room for discussion.

Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqīn) said: The truth is that their intention is that what is meant as an attribution does not necessarily take the feminine form, even if it occasionally comes in it contrary to the general rule. The well-known view is to interpret what has been mentioned as a metaphor in the predication (majāz fī al-isnād), and the original is "a life whose owner is pleased" (ʿīsha rāḍin ṣāḥibuhā), so the contentment was attributed to the life because, through its perpetual purity from impurities, it is as if it were itself pleased. He also permitted that there may be in it a metaphor that is both implicit (makniyya) and imaginative (takhyīliyya), as is detailed in the extended works on the sciences of rhetoric (maʿānī).

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, elevated in place, because it is in the heavens, so the attribution of height to it is literal. It is also permissible that it be figurative, while it is literal in respect of its ranks and what is in it of buildings and the like. Or there is an omitted modifier, meaning: lofty in its ranks, or its buildings, or its trees. In the sea (al-Bahr, i.e., the commentary of Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is "lofty" in place and in rank, and the discussion involved in using "lofty" for both is not hidden.

"Its fruits (qutufuha)" — the plural of qitf, with a kasra on the qaf, which is what is plucked from fruit. Some scholars added: "quickly." It seems that this is because it is the nature of the qatf (with a fatha on the qaf), which is the verbal noun of qatafa. They did not make qutufuha its plural, because the plural of a verbal noun is not regular. And [this is in keeping with] His saying, exalted is He, "near (daniyah)," meaning close: a man can pick from it while standing, as al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, said.

Some scholars said: "The standing person, the seated person, and the reclining person can reach it with their mouths from its tree." On this basis, it is possible that al-Bara's meaning was a figurative illustration. 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah that he said: "It has drawn near, so nothing will push their hands away from it, nor any thorn." On this reading, the nearness (dunuw) was explained as ease of reaching.

﴿Kuloo wa-ishraboo﴾ (Eat and drink) is governed by an implied verb of saying (idmar al-qawl), meaning: it will be said to them therein, that. The plural pronoun is used in consideration of the meaning (ri'ayat al-ma'na). ﴿Hani'an﴾ (wholesome, without hardship) is an adjective (sifah) of an omitted noun that stands as the direct object (maf'ul bihi). The original sense is "eating and drinking, wholesome," meaning without any disturbance. The object was omitted, and its adjective was put in its place. It is valid to make it an adjective of that omitted noun even though it is applied to more than one, because fa'il (the form hani'an) is used for the singular and for what is above it without change. Some scholars made the omitted word a verbal noun (masdar), and likewise its adjective, namely ﴿hani'an﴾. The reason it is not dualized is that the masdar also applies to the dual. So do not be heedless of this.

It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) for a verb of its own root. Fa'il is among the patterns of verbal nouns just as it is among the patterns of adjectives. That is, "you were given wholesome well-being" (hunni'tum hani'an). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), and discussion of such clauses is well known.

﴿Bima asslaftum﴾ (for what you sent forward) is in exchange for what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿Fi al-ayyam al-khaliyah﴾ (in the days that have passed) means the past days, which are the days of this world. It was said: "the days empty of delights," meaning the real ones, which are also the days of this world. It was said: "the days that you emptied of carnal desires." On this reading is based what is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Waki' about interpreting these days as the days of fasting.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ya'qub al-Hanafi, who said: "It has reached me that on the Day of Resurrection Allah, exalted is He, will say: 'O My friends, how often I looked upon you in the world, while your lips were dried of drinks, your eyes were sunken, and your stomachs were hollow. So be now in your bliss. (Eat and drink, wholesome, for what you sent forward in the days that have passed.)'"

The apparent meaning is that what is based on interpreting the days that have passed as the days of fasting is not restricted to that, and the generality is what is apparent in the verse.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verses 25–27:**

﴿And as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, would that I had not been given my record, and had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾

Page 49

Because of what he sees of the ugliness of his deeds and the clear exposure of the reckoning, which distresses him, he says: "Oh, ﴿would that it﴾," i.e., the death that I died in the world, "﴿had been the decisive one﴾," i.e., the one that cut off my affair, so that I would not have been raised up after it and would not have been created to face what I now face. The pronoun in ﴿لَيْتَها﴾ refers to "the death" (al-mawta), which the context indicates even though it has not been mentioned before.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the state he witnessed, i.e., "would that this state had been the death that ended me," because he found it more bitter than death, so he wished for death at that point. It has been said: "The worst of death is that at which one wishes for death."

It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to the worldly life understood from the context, and that the intended meaning of ﴿al-qāḍiyah (the decisive one)﴾ is death, for it is well known in that usage. That is: "Would that the worldly life had been death, and I had not been created alive." By interpreting ﴿al-qāḍiyah﴾ in the manner mentioned, the objection is dispelled that it requires a renewed matter, whereas there is no renewal in continuing in non-existence. Indeed, this view is not free from remoteness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 28:

﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾. That is, what was mine in the world of wealth and the like, such as followers (al-ittiba'), has not availed me anything. This is on the basis that the "ma" in ﴿mā aghnā﴾ is negative (nafiyah). The "ma" in "māliyah" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), the subject of (aghnā), and its object is omitted; and "liyah" is a prepositional phrase (jarr and majrur) in the position of the relative clause (ṣilah). It is also permissible to take (māliyah) as an expression for "wealth" (māl) attached to the first person pronoun suffix (yā' al-mutakallim). The first view is more comprehensive in covering the followers (al-ittiba') and the like, since this consideration cannot be achieved on the second view except through the notion of necessity (al-luzum). It is also permissible for the "ma" in "mā aghnā" to be interrogative (istifhamiyyah) for denial (li'l-inkar), and "māliyah" would then be on the basis of a possibility, meaning: what thing has my wealth availed me?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 29:

﴿Halaka ʿannī sulṭāniyah﴾ — that is: my proof, with which I used to argue in the world, has been nullified. This is how Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddi and most of the early scholars (al-salaf) explained it. Or [it means]: my dominion and my power over people, and I remain poor and humiliated. Or [it means]: my power over the faculties and instruments that were created for me, so that I was unable to use them in acts of obedience. He says this out of regret and sorrow. Qatadah also took this view, pointing to the reason for preferring it over the second [interpretation]. ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him that he said: "By God, not everyone who enters the Fire was a ruler of a town. Rather, God created them and gave them power over their bodies, commanded them to obey Him, and forbade them to disobey Him." Indicating this, he also preferred the first interpretation over the second. However, it has been said that what follows (the rest of the verse) is more fitting to it, and God willing, you will become acquainted with that.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad. It is also related about Fanakhsru, known as ʿAḍud al-Dawlah, the son of Buwayh, that when he recited his verse:

"Drinking from the cup is only in the rain, and in the song of maidens at dawn,

Bewitching women who strip away reason, delicate ones amid the strings of the lute,

Displaying the cups from their dawning, pouring the wine for whoever surpasses mankind,

ʿAḍud al-Dawlah and the son of his pillar, king of kings, conqueror of destiny,"

he did not prosper after it and went mad, and his tongue would not move except with this verse. In the Yatimah of al-Thaʿalibi it is stated that when he was dying, his tongue would not move except to recite: ﴿What my wealth has not availed me﴾ and ﴿My authority has perished from me﴾. It is narrated from Abu ʿAmr that the silent hā' (hā' al-sakt) of ﴿māliyah﴾ was assimilated into the hā' of ﴿halaka﴾. This is weak by analogy, because the hā' al-sakt is not assimilated when pausing upon it is either realized or presumed, as in Sharh al-Tawdih. In that same work, there is a transmission of assimilation in what was mentioned from Warsh, and it has been objected that what is transmitted from him is only the transfer (naql) in ﴿kitābiyah﴾. And God Most High knows best.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 32:**

﴿Then, in a chain whose length is﴾, that is, its measure and the extent of its length, ﴿seventy cubits﴾. It is permissible that this be understood literally, as the known number, and God Most High knows best the wisdom in its being this number.

It is also permissible that it be meant as an expression of abundance, since seven and seventy are frequently used for abundance and hyperbole. This was preferred on the ground that it is more eloquent than keeping it to its literal sense. The word *dhirāʿ* (cubit) is feminine. Ibn al-Shiḥna said: some of the tribe of ʿUkl used it as masculine, so they say *al-thawb khamsu adhraʿin wa khamsatu adhraʿin* (the garment is five cubits and five cubits). What is meant is the cubit known among the Arabs, which is the forearm cubit (*dhirāʿ al-yad*), because God, glorified is He, addressed them only in terms they know.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj and Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said: it is the cubit of the king (*dhirāʿ al-malik*). Ibn al-Mubarak and a group transmitted from Nawf al-Bakkālī that he said, while he was then in Kufa: "The cubit is seventy spans (*bāʿ*), and the span is the distance between you and Mecca." This requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: God knows best which cubit it is.

The *silsila* (chain) is links, each one passing through another lengthwise, as if it were derived from *tasalsul al-shayʾ* (the thing being disturbed or set in motion). Its *tanwīn* (nunation, the final "-n" sound in "silsilatin") is for magnification (*tafkhīm*). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "If one of its links were placed upon a mountain, it would melt like lead."

﴿Then thread it﴾, that is, enter it, as in His saying ﴿then He threaded it as springs in the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. Its entering into them is that it is wound around his body and coiled around him from all directions, so that he remains constricted within it, unable to move at all.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the people of the Fire will be in it like the *thaʿlab* in the *jubba*. The *thaʿlab* is the tip of the spear shaft, and the *jubba* is the *zajj* (the iron butt-end of the spear).

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn Jurayj that he said: Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The chain enters through his backside, then comes out from his mouth, and then they are strung upon it as locusts are strung upon a stick, and then they are roasted."

In another report transmitted from them, it is threaded into his rear until it comes out of his nostrils. From this it has been said that there is inversion (*qalb*) in the verse, and the original would be *fa-usluku hā fīhi* (thread them in it). The majority hold to the apparent sense. The *fāʾ* is a conditional response (*jazāʾiyya*), as in His saying ﴿and your Lord, so magnify﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 3]. The implied sense is: "Whatever the case may be, thread him in a chain, etc." The adverbial phrase and what accompanies it were fronted as a substitute for the omitted element, and so that the *fāʾ* would stand in the middle, as is its proper place, and to indicate restriction, as if it were said: "Do not thread him except in this chain," since it is more dreadful than the other places of constriction in the Blazing Fire.

It is also permissible that the sense be as follows: "Then, whatever the case may be, in a chain whose length is seventy cubits, thread him." In that case there are two fronting operations: fronting the adverbial phrase before the verb to indicate restriction, and fronting it before the *fāʾ* after deleting the conditional particle as compensation. The placement of *thumma* (then) in both places is to indicate the difference between the kinds of punishment they suffer: the shackling, the burning, and the threading, according to what a group has chosen. Some permitted that *thumma* be taken in its literal sense of indicating a interval of time, but the first view was preferred on the ground that it is more fitting to the context of threat.

Some claimed that the second *thumma* conjoins an implied utterance with what was implied before it, namely *khudhūhu* (seize him), to indicate the difference between the two commands, and the *fāʾ* in *fa-usluku hu* conjoins the spoken words with the spoken words, so that two conjunctive particles do not follow one conjoined element. This requires that the chain be fronted before the *fāʾ* after deleting the utterance, so that the aforementioned overlap does not arise. The basis of this strained view is a hasty heedlessness of what we have mentioned, so do not be heedless. From this it becomes known that the claim that there is nothing in the verse that indicates restriction is weak, because ﴿in a chain﴾ is not the object of *usluku hu* (thread him), so that there is not a combination of two conjunctive particles; rather it is the object of an omitted element, which is therefore assumed to be placed before the original order. And the fronting of the Blazing Fire serves as an indication that ﴿in a chain﴾ is fronted before its governing element.

Verse 33: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty.﴾ This is an explanatory clause in the manner of a resumptive statement (istinaf), for emphasis, as if it were said: "Why did he deserve this?" So it is answered: "Because he was, in the world, persistently upon disbelief in Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty." It has also been said: that is, in the knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, which relates to things as they are in reality, that he would not be characterized by belief in Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. The first is the apparent meaning. The mention of ﴿the Mighty﴾ serves to indicate the reason for the greatness of his punishment. It has also been said that it is to convey that He, Mighty and Majestic is He, is the One who deserves greatness alone, so whoever attributes greatness to himself deserves the most severe punishments.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 34:

﴿And does not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾ That is: and does not urge the giving of his food, which the needy person deserves, from the wealth of the affluent. Thus there is an elided genitive construction (mudaf muqaddar), because urging (hath) applies only to an action, and food (ta'am) is not an action. It is also permissible that "food" (ta'am) carries the meaning of "feeding" (it'am), by placing the noun in the position of the verbal noun (masdar), as in "giving" (ata') meaning "giving" (i'ta'). That is: and does not urge the feeding of the needy, let alone giving away what he owns. Thus there is no elided genitive construction. It has been said that urging (hath) is mentioned to indicate that one who abandons urging is in this rank, so how much more so one who abandons the action itself. How fine is the saying of Zaynab al-Thirriyya, lamenting her brother Yazid:

When guests arrive, he is a helper to the tribe, whose cooking pots are never idle.

She means his urging of them to hospitality and his hastening them, and his being sharp with them (in generosity). In this there are several aspects of praise. Abu al-Darda', may Allah be pleased with him, used to urge his wife to make plenty of broth for the sake of the needy, and he would say: "We removed half of the chain by faith; shall we not remove its other half?" He drew this from the verse, for he made the deserving of the chain conditional upon the absence of faith and the absence of urging. The specific mention of these two matters is said to be because the most hideous of beliefs is disbelief, and the most abominable of vices is miserliness and hardness of heart. The verse also indicates that disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (furu'), like the rule concerning the prohibition of... Otherwise they would not be punished for abandoning urging to feed the needy.

﴿So he will have no close friend here today﴾, a sympathetic one who would protect him and ward off harm from him, because his friends will avoid him and flee from him. ﴿Nor any food except from ghislin (a pus-like discharge)﴾. The lexicographers said: it is what flows from wounds when they are washed, from the verb ghasala (to wash), on the pattern fi‘lin. Ibn 'Abbas said, in the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir through the route of Ikrimah from him, that it is the blood and water that flow from the flesh of the people of the Fire. Its meaning is similar in his narration reported by them both through the route of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from him: it is the pus of the people of the Fire.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported through a route from him that he said: "I do not know what ghislin is, but I think it is the zaqqum." However, most scholars hold the first view.

al-Hakim reported, and declared it authentic, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If a bucketful of ghislin were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

Some scholars made it identical with al-dari‘ (the thorny plant). Others said: "They are two different things." The discussion of this will come, God willing. It has a predicate (khabar) of laysa, and al-Mahdawi said: "It is not valid for the phrase ﴿ها هُنا﴾ (here) to be the predicate." He did not explain what prevents this. al-Qurtubi followed him in this, and said: "Because the meaning would become: there is no food here ﴿except from ghislin﴾, and this is not valid, because there is other food besides it."

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying: "If there is other food besides it, and the eating is a different kind of eating, then the restriction (hasr) is valid with respect to the difference between the two kinds of eating."

As for if al-dari‘ is ghislin, as some have said, then there is no contradiction between this restriction and the restriction in His saying, ﴿They will have no food except from dari‘﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6], since the thing restricted in both verses is from one and the same thing. What prevents this is for a reason other than the one he mentioned, namely: if we make ﴿ها هُنا﴾ the predicate, then ﴿لَهُ﴾ (for him) and ﴿اليَوْمَ﴾ (today) would be dependent on what the predicate depends on, which is the governing element in ﴿ها هُنا﴾. This governing element is a implied (ma‘nawi) one, so its complement may not precede it. But if the governing element were verbal (lafzi), it would be permissible, as in His saying, ﴿and there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4], where ﴿لَهُ﴾ depends on ﴿كُفُوًا﴾, and it is the predicate of ﴿يَكُنْ﴾. End of quote. Yet applying the term "implied governing element" (al-‘amil al-ma‘nawi) to the dependent phrase of a prepositional phrase whose verb is omitted requires examination.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 37:

﴿None shall eat it except the sinners﴾. The sinners (aṣḥāb al-khaṭāyā) are those who derive from khaṭi'a (to sin), when a man deliberately commits a sin, not from khaṭa' (error), which is the opposite of correctness (ṣawāb), nor the opposite of intention (ʿamd). It is said, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, that they are the polytheists. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, al-ʿAtakī, and Ṭalḥa, in one narration, read "al-khāṭiyūn" with a damma-marked yāʾ replacing the hamza. Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, Ṭalḥa in another narration, and Nāfiʿ with a variant from him, read "al-khāṭūn" with the hamza dropped after being changed for lightness, on the basis that it derives from khaṭiʾa, like the reading of whoever pronounced the hamza. And from Ibn ʿAbbās there is something that indicates rejection of this.

al-Ḥākim recorded it and authenticated it, through the route of Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, from him, that he said: "What is al-khāṭūn? It is only al-khāṭiʾūn. What is al-ṣābūn? It was also said that it derives from khaṭā yakhṭū, so the intended meaning is those who step over from obedience to disobedience and from truth to falsehood, and transgress the limits of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is then a metaphor for sinners too.

These are the apparent meanings of these verses: the believing obedient person is given his book in his right hand, and the disbeliever is given his book in his left hand. Nothing is known from them about the state of the corrupt person who died in his corruption without repentance. Indeed it was said that there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an about his state, and his matter has been disputed. Al-Māwardī affirmed that the well-known view is that he is given his book in his right hand, then he related an opinion of suspension (waqf), and said: no one holds that he is given it in his left hand. Yūsuf ibn ʿUmar said: it has been disputed concerning the disobedient believers; it was said they take their books in their right hands, and it was said in their left hands. The earlier scholars differed: it was said they take them before entering the Fire, and this would be a sign that they will not abide in it forever.

It was also said they take them after leaving it. Among the people of knowledge are those who suspended judgement because of the conflict of texts, and whoever memorises a proof is a proof over whoever does not memorise it, and the affirmative is given precedence over the negative. Furthermore, there is no explicit statement in these verses that the servant reads his book, and what is reported on that matter varies. What gathers the verses and the hadiths, according to what al-Laqānī said, is that among those who take them are those who do not read their book, because it contains disgraces, ugly deeds, crimes and scandals, so the amazement and terror seize him and he cannot distinguish anything, like the disbeliever. Among them are those who read it themselves, and among them are those who call the people present to hear its reading, out of admiration for what is in it. The apparent sense of the texts is that reading is literal, though it was said it is figurative, expressing knowledge; but this is not correct.

The wording of al-Ḥasan: "Every person reads his book, whether he was unlettered or not." The apparent sense of the reports is that good deeds are written distinct from bad deeds. It was said that the bad deeds of the believer come at the beginning and end of his book: "These are your sins, I have covered them and forgiven them," and the good deeds of the disbeliever come at the beginning and end of his book: "These are your good deeds, I have returned them to you and did not accept them." It was also said that the believer reads his own bad deeds, and people read his good deeds until they say, "What is this servant's bad deed?" and he says, "What is my good deed?"

It was also said that each reads his good and bad deeds, and the first line of the believer's book is white, so when he reads it his face becomes bright, while the disbeliever is the opposite. The apparent sense of the verses and hadiths is that the giving of books is not restricted to this nation, although some scholars hesitated about this because some of them give an indication of restriction.

In a hadith narrated by Aḥmad from Abū al-Dardāʾ, that a man said to him: "How do you recognise your nation among the nations from Noah, peace be upon him, until your nation, O Messenger of Allah?" He (ﷺ) said: "They are radiant, with white marks from the traces of ablution; no one else is like that, and I recognise them: they are given their books in their right hands." The hadith.

This has been mentioned earlier, so recall it. The truth is that the jinn in these matters have the same ruling as humans, as al-Qurṭubī investigated and others stated explicitly. Yes, the prophets and angels, upon them be blessings and peace, do not take a book. Indeed the seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning, among them Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, also do not take a book. The first to be given his book in his right hand will have a radiance like the radiance of the sun: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, as in the hadith; after him Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Asad; and the first to take his book in his left hand is his brother al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, whose mention has passed not long ago. The reports concerning the manner in which the books reach their owners vary.

It has been reported that the wind carries them from a treasury beneath the Throne, so no book misses the neck of its owner.

It has also been reported that everyone is called and given his book, and the reconciliation is by the angels taking them from their necks and placing them in their hands.

And Allah knows best. The full discussion of this matter is to be sought in its proper place.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and by what you do not see﴾.
