Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 40–41:

﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾, one who conveys it from Allah, exalted is He, for a messenger does not speak from himself. ﴿Noble﴾ in the sight of Allah, mighty and majestic, and he is the Prophet (ﷺ) according to the majority of scholars. Ibn al-Sa'ib, Muqatil and Ibn Qutaybah said that he is Jibril (peace be upon him). And the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and it is not the word of a poet﴾, etc. It has been said that this is evidence for what the majority said, because the meaning is to affirm that he
Page 53
(peace and blessings be upon him) is a messenger, not a poet or a soothsayer, as the occasion of revelation indicates. The clarification of this is that they did not say of Jibril (peace be upon him) that he was such-and-such; rather they said it of the Prophet (ﷺ). So if "a noble messenger" were meant to be Jibril (peace be upon him), the contrast would be lost and the conjunction would not be appropriate, just as you would say "indeed it is the word of a scholar, and it is not the word of an ignorant person." And if you said "and it is not the word of a brave man," you would be attributing to him something disliked. Some scholars objected to this, saying: this is correct if it is granted that the meaning is to affirm a messenger, not a poet, and that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ is not the word of a poet, as an affirmation of the messengerhood by way of allusion. But if the purpose from the context is taken to be the affirmation of the truth of the revelation and that it is from Allah, exalted and majestic is He, then it is a reminder to these people and a regret for their opponents, and it is in itself truth and certainty, with no doubt hovering around it, as what follows indicates.

So the second view also has a fine placement, and it is as if it were said: this Qur'an is indeed the word of Jibril, the noble messenger, and it is not from the side of Muhammad (ﷺ) as you claim and allege that he is a poet and a soothsayer. In this case he (ﷺ) would have been cleared of poetry and soothsaying by way of incidental implication (idmaj). End. And this is a fine verification.

﴿Little is it that you believe﴾: that is, you affirm with little affirmation. ﴿Little﴾ is an adjective of the absolute object of ﴿you believe﴾, and "ma" is extra for emphasis. The littleness is in its apparent meaning, for because of the clear truthfulness of him (ﷺ), their affirmation of him, peace and blessings be upon him, was necessary in general, even if they showed the opposite out of obstinacy and refused with their tongues out of rebellion. Al-Zamakhshari took "littleness" to mean non-existence and negation, i.e., you do not believe at all, and there is nothing in this except that it is weaker than the first in apparentness.

Abu Hayyan said: "Qalilan" is not meant here as pure negation as he claimed, for that occurs only with "aqallu" as in "aqallu rajulin yaqulu kadha illa Zaydun," and with "qalla" as in "qalla rajulun yaqulu kadha illa Zaydun." It may also occur with "qalil" and "qalilah" when they are in the nominative, as in what they permitted in the verse of the poet:

"It was made to kneel, then it cast a settlement upon a settlement, little are the voices in it except its lowing."
But when it is in the accusative, as in "qalilan darabtu" or "qalilan ma darabtu," on the basis that "ma" is verbal, that is not permitted, because in "qalilan darabtu" it is in the accusative governed by "darabtu," and the Arabs did not use "qalilan" when it is governed by a negated verb, but only as the opposite of "kathir." As for "qalilan ma darabtu" with "ma" as verbal, it requires "qalil" in the nominative, because the verbal "ma" is in the nominative position as a subject of inception. End.

You know that such a thing is not to be heard from someone like al-Zamakhshari without evidence, for the apparent sense is that he did not say what he said except after careful consideration, and he is the knight of the field of Arabic grammar. He permitted it to be an adjective of an omitted time, i.e., "a little time you believe," and that, as it is said, is when they are asked who created them or who created the heavens and the earth, for then they say: Allah, exalted is He. Ibn Atiyyah said: "Qalilan" is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minun," and it may be that "ma" is negating, so their belief is wholly negated, and it may be that it is verbal, and what is characterized by littleness is linguistic belief, and they affirmed some slight things which do not avail them anything, such as the maintaining of kinship and chastity, which he (peace and blessings be upon him) used to command, as true and right. End.

It has been objected that it is not valid to put "qalilan" in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "tu'minun," because either "ma" with it is negating, and then the verb negated by "ma" may not be omitted, and likewise omitting "ma"; so it is not permitted to say "zaydan ma adribuhu" on the estimate of "ma adribu zaydan ma adribuhu." If it is verbal, it would be in the nominative position as the agent of "qalilan," meaning "qalilan imanukum," and this is refuted by the requirement of its governing without a preceding element on which it depends, and its accusative has no governor. Or it is in the nominative position as the subject of inception, and this is refuted by the requirement that it be a subject without a predicate, since what precedes it is accusative, not nominative. So consider this carefully. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu 'Amr (in one narration from them) and al-Hasan and al-Jahdari read "yu'minun" with the yaa' (third person), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 42:

﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾, as you claim, [but] once more: ﴿little do you take heed﴾. That is, you take heed only a little, and therefore the matter is confused for you. The full discussion of its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is like the discussion of what precedes it, and likewise the recitation. The mention of belief together with the negation of poetry, and of taking heed together with the negation of soothsaying, has been said to be because the fact that the Qur'an does not resemble poetry is a clear matter that none denies except a stubborn person. So there is no excuse for one who claims it (that the Qur'an is poetry) in abandoning belief, and he is more disbelieving than a donkey. This is unlike its distinction from soothsaying, for that depends on taking heed of his (ﷺ) circumstances, and of the meanings of the Qur'an that contradict the way of soothsaying, and of the meanings of their statements. It has been objected that this too definitely depends on reflection. It is answered that for the purpose it suffices that the difference between them is that the dependence of the first is not like the dependence of the second.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verse 43–44:

﴿A revelation﴾, i.e., it is a revelation ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾. He (glory be to Him) sent it down through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him). Abu al-Sammal read «تَنْزِيلًا» (tanzilan) in the accusative, with the implied verb "nazzalahu" (He sent it down) as its governing verb, meaning "He sent it down as a revelation." ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾. Al-taqawwul (fabrication) is false attribution, and it is called taqawwul because it is contrived speech. Al-aqawil (the fabricated sayings) are the fabricated statements. It is the plural of qawl (saying) in an irregular pattern (ʿala ghayr al-qiyas), or it is the plural of aqwal (sayings), so it is a plural of a plural, like anaʿim, the plural of anʿam, and ababit, the plural of abyat.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said that the fabricated sayings are called aqawil as a diminutive and belittling form of them, like your saying al-aʿajib (the wonders) and al-adahik (the jokes), as though they were the plural of uf'ula derived from qawl. Ibn al-Munir criticised this, saying that uf'ula derived from qawl is unusual with respect to morphological (tasrifi) analysis. It is answered that this objection does not apply, because his meaning is that it is a plural of a singular that is not in use, since there is no basis for restricting it to fabrication other than what was mentioned. The better view is to say that it is not restricted to fabrication by its coinage, and that it is a plural as you have heard. The diminutive and belittling sense comes from the context, and the meaning is: if he had claimed against Us something that We did not say.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verses 45–46:

﴿La-akhadhna minhu﴾ means: We would have seized him. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿bil-yamin﴾ means: an explanation with His right hand after the general term, as in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]. ﴿Then We would have cut from him the jugular vein﴾ means: his jugular vein (al-watin). It is, as Ibn 'Abbas said, the tendon of the heart (niyat al-qalb), which, if it is severed, its owner dies. Mujahid reported that it is the cord in the back, which is the spinal marrow (al-nukha'). Al-Kalbi said it is a vein between al-'ilba' (the sinew of the neck) and the windpipe (al-hulqum). It has also been said that it is a thick vein that the cutting blade of the slaughterer reaches. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh ibn Dirar:

When 'Arrabah brings me near and carries my saddle, then gasp with the blood of the jugular vein.

This is a depiction of destruction by the most horrific means that kings employ against those with whom they are angry: that one takes the executioner by his right hand, strikes him with the sword, and cuts off his neck.

It is reported from al-Hasan that the meaning is: "We would have cut off his right hand, then We would have cut his jugular vein," as a lesson and a deterrent, and the ba' in ʿalayhi is superfluous. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that al-yamin means power, and the meaning is that he is seized with force and severity. This is weak, because it involves the use of a metaphor without benefit, and it loses in it the depiction, the detail, and the summary, and it becomes superfluous with no purpose.

Dhakwan and his son Muhammad read ﴿wa-law yuqawwilu﴾ as an imperfect verb. He said: it was also read ﴿wa-law tuqawwila﴾ in the passive voice, so the subject-substitute is ﴿ba'd﴾; if it was read in the nominative, then it is so, and if it was read in the accusative, then it is ʿalayna.

Dhakwan and his son Muhammad read ﴿wa-law yuqawwilu﴾ as an imperfect verb. He said: it was also read ﴿wa-law tuqawwila﴾ in the passive voice, so the subject-substitute is ﴿ba'd﴾; if it was read in the nominative, then it is so, and if it was read in the accusative, then it is ʿalayna.

﴿So none of you﴾, O people, ﴿could hold back from him any one﴾, i.e., from this act, which is killing, ﴿restraining﴾, i.e., preventing. The meaning is that no one can be prevented from killing him. He preferred the view that the pronoun in (عَنْهُ, "from him") refers back to the one to whom the pronoun in (تَقَوَّلَ, "he invented") refers. The meaning is: no one can come between us and him.

The apparent reading of ﴿حاجِزِينَ﴾ (ḥājizīn, "restraining") is that it is the predicate (khabar, the complement of the subject) of (مَا, "not"), according to the dialect of the Ḥijāzīs (lughat al-Ḥijāziyyīn, the Hijazi dialect of Arabic), because it is the point where the benefit of the sentence lies. The (مِنْ, "min") is superfluous (zāʾida, extra, having no independent meaning). (أَحَدٍ, "aḥad," "any one") is its noun (ism, the subject of the negated verbal sentence). (مِنكم, "minkum," "of you") is said to be in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) relative to it, because if it had come after it, it would have been a qualifier (ṣifa) of it. Since it came before, it is parsed as a ḥāl, as is common with the qualifier of an indefinite noun when it precedes it, and this was examined. It was also said that it is for clarification (lil-bayān), or that it is connected to (حاجِزِينَ), as you say (مَا فِيكَ زَيْدٌ راغِبًا, "there is no Zayd in you desiring," i.e., "Zayd is not in you desiring").

This separation does not prevent the accusative of the predicate of (مَا).

Al-Ḥawfī and others said that (حاجِزِينَ) is a qualifier (naʿt) of (أَحَدٍ), and is pluralized according to meaning, because it carries the sense of a group. It occurs in general negation for the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. Among its examples is the verse, ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 285], and ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾ [Al-Aḥzāb: 32]. Thus (أَحَدٌ) is the subject (mubtadaʾ) and the predicate is (مِنكم, "of you"). This view has been judged weak, because the negation governs the predicate, which is its being "of you," so it does not govern the restraining, although it is more appropriate for it to govern that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verses 48–50:

﴿And indeed it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from it. ﴿And indeed We know that among you are deniers﴾, so We will recompense them for their denial. It has also been said that the address is to the Muslims, and the meaning is that among them are people who will disbelieve in the Qur'an. ﴿And indeed it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿is a great regret for the disbelievers﴾, when they witness the reward of the believers. Muqatil said: "Indeed their denial of the Qur'an is a regret upon them." So he returned the pronoun to the verbal noun (masdar) implied by His words, ﴿deniers﴾. The first view is more apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 69, verses 51–52:

﴿And indeed, it﴾ — i.e., the Qur'an — ﴿is the truth of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn)﴾. That is, the truth of certainty belongs to certainty (li-l-yaqīn ḥaqq al-yaqīn), and the meaning is "the very essence of certainty" (la-ʿayn al-yaqīn). It is thus like the very self and essence of a thing (ʿayn al-shayʾ wa-nafsihi). The idāfa (genitive construction) here carries the sense of lām (of/for), as has been explicitly stated in al-Kashshāf. It is also permitted that the idāfa be in the sense of min (from/of), i.e., "the established truth from certainty." This has already been discussed under Surah al-Wāqiʿa, and what is useful here may be found there, so refer back to it.

Some of the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, have mentioned that the highest of the degrees of knowledge is ḥaqq al-yaqīn (the truth of certainty), below it is ʿayn al-yaqīn (the eye of certainty), and below that is ʿilm al-yaqīn (the knowledge of certainty). The first is like the knowledge of the intelligent person about death when he tastes it; the second is like his knowledge of it at the moment of witnessing its angels, peace be upon them;

and the third is like his knowledge of it at all other times. The full discussion of this is to be sought in their books.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ — i.e., glorify God Most High by mentioning His mighty name, declaring Him transcendent above being pleased with the fabrication of falsehood against Him, and giving thanks for what He has revealed to you of this Qur'an, which is of exalted station. Something similar has also passed under Surah al-Wāqiʿa, so return to it if you wish. And God Most High is the Granter of success.
